script.opening: "Hi — cheers. I just need a fit note really, work’s been doing my head in and I need a bit of time off. I’m not sleeping, I’m exhausted, I can’t focus. If you could just sign me off for a couple of weeks that’d be great and I’ll be out of your way. It’s nothing major, just stress, everyone’s stressed aren’t they."

facts.text: If explored: pervasive low mood and anhedonia for ~3 months, early-morning waking, unintentional weight loss, poor concentration, social withdrawal, stopped activities he loved (football). Meets the picture of a more severe depressive episode (NICE NG222 (2022, updated December 2025) grades depression as less severe or more severe), not just "work stress".

On gentle questioning: a painful relationship breakup ~3 months ago; drinking more, alone, to cope; feels he’s "failing" and "a burden". The "sick note for work stress" reframes a depressive illness into something less stigmatised.

CRITICAL: on sensitive, explicit questioning he discloses passive thoughts that "everyone would be better off without me" and fleeting thoughts of not wanting to wake up — but, if explored carefully, no current active plan/intent/means and some protective factors (his mum, his dog, would never want to hurt his family). Risk MUST be asked about directly — the sick-note request must not be processed without it.

HIDDEN AGENDA — he came for a sick note as a "legitimate" reason to be seen, because he can’t bring himself to say "I think I’m depressed" or "I’ve been having dark thoughts" — male stigma and shame. The quick note request is partly a test of whether the doctor will look past it. If the GP just signs the note and ends the consult, the depression and the risk are missed entirely.

Officially: a quick fit note for work stress. What he needs: recognition of depression behind the request, an explicit suicide-risk assessment, validation that lets him drop the "just stress" framing, and a proper treatment/safety plan — the note being the door, not the consultation.

ice.ideas: It’s just work stress; a sick note and some time off will sort it.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — he can’t say "I’m depressed" or "I’ve had dark thoughts" (male stigma/shame), so a sick note is his "legitimate" way in; underneath, a breakup, drinking alone, feeling a burden, and passive suicidal thoughts.
ice.expectations: A quick fit note. What he actually needs: the depression behind the request recognised, an explicit suicide-risk assessment, and a proper treatment/safety plan.

cues: "Just a sick note for stress, I’ll be out of your way" — a legitimate door for something he can’t name; don’t just process it.
3 months of anhedonia, early waking, weight loss, stopped football — depression, not stress.
Avoids eye contact, "everyone’s stressed" — minimising; the breakup, the drinking and the dark thoughts are underneath.

checkpoints.text: Looks BEYOND the sick-note request: recognises a more severe depressive episode (NICE NG222 terms) (pervasive low mood/anhedonia >2 weeks with biological features — early waking, weight loss, poor concentration, withdrawal) rather than processing "work stress" and ending the consultation

Performs an EXPLICIT SUICIDE-RISK ASSESSMENT: asks directly about thoughts of being better off dead / not wanting to wake up, active suicidal ideation, plan, intent, means, preparatory acts, and protective factors — understanding that asking does not increase risk, and (NICE NG225, 2022) without relying on risk tools or low/medium/high ratings to predict suicide

Assesses severity and context (PHQ-9-type screen, alcohol as a worsening factor, the breakup trigger, functional impact) and screens for relevant comorbidity/risk (escalating alcohol, prior self-harm)

Negotiates an evidence-based plan matched to severity (NICE NG222: for more severe depression, individual CBT combined with an antidepressant, individual CBT, behavioural activation, or an antidepressant alone, by his preference): psychological therapy (referral to NHS Talking Therapies) and/or an SSRI with informed discussion, including review within 1 week of starting it because of his suicidal thoughts, the fit note used appropriately as part of care, lifestyle/alcohol, activity and social reconnection, and follow-up
Addresses the alcohol as a depressant and risk factor, and gives appropriate advice/support without derailing the consultation into a lecture

Creates a safe, non-judgemental space that lets him drop the "just stress" framing and disclose the real picture; treats the sick-note request as the door, not the destination, and does not collude with minimisation
Handles male stigma and shame with warmth — normalising depression and help-seeking — so he engages with treatment rather than leaving with only a note

Safety-nets robustly and documents: crisis routes if thoughts intensify or a plan emerges (urgent/111 option 2/crisis team/A&E), a safety plan, early follow-up (within 1 week given his suicidal thoughts — NICE NG222 for an antidepressant start in anyone aged 18–25 or at increased risk), and clear documentation of the risk assessment

worked.txt: "I can sort a fit note — but before I do, I don’t want to just sign a form and miss how you’re actually doing. You’ve said work’s doing your head in, you’re not sleeping, can’t focus, exhausted — that’s a lot. Can I ask a bit more about how things have really been, beyond work? No rush."

"From what you’re telling me — the months of feeling flat, waking at 4am, losing your appetite, packing in the football you used to love, pulling away from mates — that’s more than stress. That’s depression, and I want to say clearly: it’s an illness, not a weakness, and it’s really common in blokes your age. You’re not failing."

"I’m going to ask you something directly, because I ask everyone who feels this low and it matters. When things are this heavy — have you had thoughts that you’d be better off not here, or that others would be better off without you? … Thank you for being honest. And have those thoughts gone any further — thinking about how, or making any plans, or anything to act on it? … What stops you, on the worst days?"

"I’m really glad you told me — that took guts, and saying it out loud is genuinely a step that helps. You’re not a burden, and the fact you’ve got your mum and your dog in your mind on the bad days matters; we build on exactly that."

"One honest thing — the drinking alone, I get why, but alcohol is a depressant and it deepens this and the dark thoughts, so easing off it is part of getting better, and I’ll help. For the depression itself: I’d suggest talking therapy, which I can refer you to, and we can talk about an antidepressant if you want one — if you start one, I’ll check in with you after a week, because the first weeks matter. The fit note is part of the plan, not the whole of it — time off plus actual support."

"This matters: if those thoughts get stronger, or you find yourself thinking about how or when, I want you to ring — I’ll give you the urgent numbers and the crisis line, and that’s a 999/A&E thing if you ever feel you can’t keep yourself safe. I don’t want to leave it long — let’s talk again within a week, sooner if things get worse. You came in for a note; what you’re leaving with is a plan and people in your corner."

f.learning: A request for "a sick note for work stress" in a withdrawn young man can be the only door he can bring himself to open. The skill is to look beyond the request: recognise the more severe depressive episode (NICE NG222 (2022, updated December 2025) terms; pervasive low mood/anhedonia >2 weeks with biological features — early waking, weight loss, poor concentration, withdrawal, loss of valued activities) and NOT simply process the note and end the consultation. The non-negotiable task is an EXPLICIT suicide-risk assessment — ask directly about thoughts of being better off dead, active ideation, plan, intent, means and protective factors (asking does not increase risk) — alongside severity, the relationship-breakup trigger and the alcohol that worsens both mood and risk. The examinable hidden agenda is male stigma: he cannot say "I’m depressed" or "I’ve had dark thoughts", so the note is a legitimate entry point and a test of whether the doctor looks past it. Create safety so he drops the "just stress" framing, name depression without stigma, negotiate an evidence-based plan (Talking Therapies/SSRI, the note as part of care, alcohol, reconnection), and safety-net robustly with crisis routes and follow-up within 1 week (NICE NG222); NICE NG225 (2022) warns against risk tools or risk ratings, so the risk conversation leads to a safety plan, not a score.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG222 Depression in adults (2022, updated December 2025) · NICE NG225 Self-harm (2022) · NICE CG115 Alcohol-use disorders (2011) · DVLA Assessing fitness to drive
knowledge.summary: A fit note request for “stress” can be the way into a depressive illness. Three months of low mood, anhedonia and biological symptoms is depression; ask directly about suicide before any note is signed.

points.t: Low mood or loss of interest most days for at least 2 weeks, with symptoms such as early waking, weight or appetite change, poor concentration, fatigue, worthlessness and thoughts of death. NICE NG222 grades depression as less severe or more severe; a PHQ-9 can support, but not replace, clinical judgement.

Ask directly about thoughts that life is not worth living, suicidal ideation, plans, intent, means, previous self-harm and what keeps him safe. Asking does not increase risk. NICE NG225: do not use risk tools or low, medium or high ratings to predict suicide; make a safety plan with him.

NICE NG222: discuss the options and his preference. For more severe depression, choices include individual CBT combined with an antidepressant, individual CBT, behavioural activation, or an antidepressant alone. NHS Talking Therapies accepts self-referral.

NICE NG222: review people aged 18 to 25 or at increased risk of suicide 1 week after starting or increasing the dose; others within 2 weeks. Jordan has passive suicidal thoughts, so a 1-week review applies. Consider toxicity in overdose when choosing; dose per BNF.
Drinking alone to cope worsens mood and increases risk. Use AUDIT to measure it (NICE CG115) and give brief advice. Alcohol and depression are treated together, not one after the other.

A fit note is legitimate as part of a treatment plan; “may be fit for work” with adjustments is an option. DVLA: depression with significant concentration problems, agitation or suicidal thoughts must be notified by the driver, and he should not drive while affected.

dg.d: Acknowledges the fit note request but explores before signing; lets him tell the story beyond work.
Breakup, withdrawal from friends and football, drinking alone, work, support from his mum.
Mental state assessment; PHQ-9 to support judgement; AUDIT for alcohol.
Work stress versus depressive episode versus alcohol-related low mood; considers grief after the breakup.
Direct questions on suicidal thoughts, plans, intent, means, past self-harm and protective factors.
Names depression, explains why it is more than stress, and reduces stigma.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: NHS Talking Therapies and antidepressant options (NICE NG222) with his preference; fit note as part of care.
Alcohol addressed briefly and without lecturing; driving checked (DVLA); social reconnection encouraged.
Review within a week; crisis routes named; safety plan; risk assessment documented.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Flatness, avoiding eye contact and “everyone’s stressed” are followed rather than accepted.
Idea (work stress); concern (can’t say “I’m depressed”, shame); expectation (a quick note).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — he can’t say "I’m depressed" or "I’ve had dark thoughts" (male stigma/shame), so a sick note is his "legitimate" way in; underneath, a breakup, drinking alone, feeling a burden, and passive suicidal thoughts — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hi Jordan, I’m Dr Shah. Can you hear me okay, and are you somewhere private? … What can I help with today?
model.why: Checks privacy on video and opens neutrally

model.text: I just need a fit note really. Work’s been doing my head in. Not sleeping, exhausted, can’t focus. A couple of weeks off and I’ll be out of your way. It’s just stress, everyone’s stressed.
I can help with a fit note. Before I do, I’d like to understand what’s been happening, because not sleeping and not being able to focus is a lot to carry. Is that alright?
model.why: Agrees the request is legitimate while making space to assess

model.text: Yeah, okay.
How long has it been like this? And apart from work, how has life been generally?
model.why: Open question that widens beyond work

model.text: About three months. I split up with my girlfriend around then. Long-term. Since then, I dunno. Nothing’s the same.
That’s a big loss. Are you still enjoying the things you used to, like seeing friends or sport?
Stopped football. Don’t see my mates. Can’t be bothered with anything.
What about sleep, appetite and weight?
Wake up at four and can’t get back off. Not eating much, lost weight.
How do you usually unwind in the evenings? Some people find they’re drinking more.
model.why: Asks about alcohol in a non-judgemental way

model.text: Yeah… more than I should. On my own mostly.
I ask everyone who feels this low: when things are at their worst, do you ever feel life isn’t worth living, or that people would be better off without you?
(long pause) …Sometimes. That everyone would be better off. Some nights I don’t really want to wake up.
Thank you for telling me. That can’t have been easy. Have those thoughts gone further, thinking about how you might end your life, or making any plans?
model.why: Explores active ideation and plans after acknowledging disclosure

model.text: No. No plans. I wouldn’t. It’s just a feeling.
Have you ever hurt yourself? And on the worst days, what stops you?
Never hurt myself. My mum, I suppose. And my dog. I couldn’t do that to my mum.
Those matter a lot, and we’ll build on them. You’re not a burden, Jordan. Feeling that way is part of the illness talking.
model.why: Receives the disclosure warmly and challenges the burden belief

model.text: From what you’ve told me — three months of feeling flat, waking early, weight loss, giving up football and friends, and those dark thoughts — this is more than work stress. It’s depression. It’s an illness, not a weakness, and it’s common in men your age.
model.why: Names the diagnosis with the evidence and reduces stigma

model.text: I kind of knew. I just didn’t want to say it.
That makes sense. Saying it out loud is the first step to getting better, and you’ve just done it.
model.why: Validates the hidden agenda without judgement

model.text: There are a few things that help. Talking therapy works well, and I can refer you or you can self-refer today. Some people add an antidepressant. If you chose that, I’d want to see you a week after starting. What do you think?
model.why: Shares NICE NG222 options, including early review, and invites his view

model.text: I’ll try the talking. Maybe the tablets too, if you think so.

We can decide together at the next appointment. The drinking alone: alcohol makes low mood and dark thoughts worse, so cutting back is part of getting better. I’ll do your fit note for two weeks as part of this plan, not instead of it. And if you drive, please don’t while your concentration is this poor; there are DVLA rules I can explain.
model.why: Addresses alcohol, uses the fit note as part of care and checks driving

model.text: If the thoughts get stronger, or you start thinking about how or when, ring us, or NHS 111 and choose the mental health option, day or night. If you ever feel you can’t keep yourself safe, that’s 999 or A&E. Samaritans are on 116 123. I’ll send these to you now.
model.why: Specific crisis routes in plain language

model.text: I’d like to speak again within a week. Could you tell me what we’ve agreed?
It’s depression, not just stress. Talking therapy, cut the drinking, note for two weeks, the numbers if it gets bad, and see you next week.
Spot on. You came in for a note; you’re leaving with a plan and people on your side.
model.why: Links the outcome to his original request

social.t: The breakup, withdrawal from football and friends, and drinking alone all remove protective contact. Encourage one step back towards people or activity.
Many men present with physical or practical requests rather than naming low mood. Normalising depression helps them engage.

legal.t: Self-certification covers the first 7 days of sickness; after that a fit note is needed. Consider “may be fit for work” with adjustments such as a phased return or reduced hours.
DVLA: depression with significant memory or concentration problems, agitation, behavioural disturbance or suicidal thoughts must be notified by the licence holder. Advise not driving while affected.

professional.t: Record the direct risk questions and answers, protective factors, the safety plan, crisis numbers given and the review date (NICE NG225).

Occupational health and the Access to Work mental health support service can help with a return. Depression lasting 12 months or more with a substantial effect may count as a disability under the Equality Act 2010.

community.t: NHS Talking Therapies (self-referral); NHS 111 mental health option; Samaritans 116 123; CALM (Campaign Against Living Miserably); Andy’s Man Club peer groups.

redFlags: Suicidal thoughts with a plan, intent, means or preparation
Previous self-harm, escalating alcohol, recent loss, isolation
psychosocial: Breakup of a long-term relationship three months ago
Stopped football, withdrawn from friends; work struggling
ice: Concern: feels a failure and a burden; can’t bring himself to say “depressed”

playbook.diagnosis: “Three months of feeling flat, waking at four, weight loss, giving up things you enjoy and those dark thoughts: that’s depression, not just stress. It’s an illness, and it’s treatable.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Depression is like your battery not charging any more, however long you rest. It changes sleep, appetite and how you see yourself. The right help recharges it.”

management.reflectIce: “You came in saying it’s work stress, and work matters. But I think you knew it was more, and it took courage to tell me about the dark thoughts.”
management.psychosocial: Tie the plan to what he values: his mum, his dog, getting back to football. Keep alcohol advice short and linked to his mood.
sharedPlan: NHS Talking Therapies referral or self-referral; antidepressant as an option with review 1 week after starting (NICE NG222)
Fit note for two weeks as part of treatment; consider adjustments on return
Cut down alcohol with support; one small step back to friends or football
safetyNet: NHS 111 mental health option, Samaritans 116 123, 999 or A&E if he feels unable to keep safe
Review within a week; sooner if thoughts become plans

pitfalls.intro: The trap here is the request. Candidates who process the fit note fail the station; candidates who assess but avoid the suicide question fail it too. The patterns below reflect recurring SCA feedback.

items.fail: Signs the fit note for stress and closes.
items.why: “Did not explore the presenting problem.” The depression and the risk are missed entirely.
items.fix: Agree you can help with the note, then ask how things have really been beyond work.

items.fail: Assesses mood thoroughly but never asks directly about suicide.
items.why: “Did not assess risk.” Passive suicidal thoughts are only disclosed when asked.
items.fix: Ask the direct question, then plans, intent, means, past self-harm and protective factors.

items.fail: Starts an antidepressant with review in four weeks.
items.why: NICE NG222: review within 1 week for people at increased risk of suicide.
items.fix: State the 1-week review when discussing medication, and consider overdose toxicity.

items.fail: Labels him as depressed in the first two minutes.
items.why: Premature labelling before he feels heard can make him retreat to “just stress”.
items.fix: Gather his story first, then name depression using his own words back to him.

items.fail: Reacts awkwardly or moves quickly on after the disclosure.
items.why: “Did not respond empathically to the patient’s disclosure.”
items.fix: Pause, thank him, and challenge the burden belief before moving on.

items.fail: Gives generic advice to “seek help if things get worse”.
items.why: Vague safety-netting after suicidal thoughts is a standard failing point.
items.fix: Named crisis routes, when to use each, a review within a week, and teach-back.

timeMap.d: He wants the note fast. Agree you can help, then ask for the story first.
Duration, the breakup, anhedonia, early waking, weight loss, withdrawal, drinking alone.
Life not worth living, plans, intent, means, previous self-harm, what keeps him safe.
Depression, not just stress. Illness, not weakness. Let him own it.
Talking Therapies, antidepressant option with a 1-week review, alcohol, fit note as part of care, driving. Crisis numbers. Review within a week. Teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Signs a two-week fit note for stress and ends the consultation; never asks about mood in depth or about suicide; ignores the drinking; or lectures about alcohol and misses the risk.
wordPics.pass: Recognises depression behind the request, asks directly about suicidal thoughts and plans, offers therapy and follow-up with a crisis safety-net, and issues the note.
wordPics.exc: All of that, plus he is helped to drop the “just stress” framing himself, the disclosure is received warmly, protective factors are used, the options follow NICE NG222 with the correct 1-week review, alcohol and driving are covered briefly, and he leaves with an owned plan.

avoid.dont: “Sure, I’ll sign you off for two weeks. Come back if it doesn’t settle.”
avoid.instead: “I can do a note. First, can you tell me how things have really been, beyond work?”
avoid.why: Processing the request unexamined misses the depression and the risk.

avoid.dont: “You’re not thinking of doing anything silly, are you?”
avoid.instead: “Do you ever feel life isn’t worth living, or that people would be better off without you?”
avoid.why: A leading, minimising question invites “no”. A clear, direct question invites the truth.

avoid.dont: “You need to stop drinking — it’s making everything worse.”
avoid.instead: “Alcohol tends to deepen low mood and dark thoughts, so cutting back is part of getting better. I can help.”
avoid.why: Linking alcohol to his goal works better than an instruction.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A fit note request for “stress” can be the way into a depressive illness. Three months of low mood, anhedonia and biological symptoms is depression; ask directly about suicide before any note is signed.

points.t: Low mood or loss of interest most days for at least 2 weeks, with symptoms such as early waking, weight or appetite change, poor concentration, fatigue, worthlessness and thoughts of death. NICE NG222 grades depression as less severe or more severe; a PHQ-9 can support, but not replace, clinical judgement.

Ask directly about thoughts that life is not worth living, suicidal ideation, plans, intent, means, previous self-harm and what keeps him safe. Asking does not increase risk. NICE NG225: do not use risk tools or low, medium or high ratings to predict suicide; make a safety plan with him.

NICE NG222: discuss the options and his preference. For more severe depression, choices include individual CBT combined with an antidepressant, individual CBT, behavioural activation, or an antidepressant alone. NHS Talking Therapies accepts self-referral.

NICE NG222: review people aged 18 to 25 or at increased risk of suicide 1 week after starting or increasing the dose; others within 2 weeks. Jordan has passive suicidal thoughts, so a 1-week review applies. Consider toxicity in overdose when choosing; dose per BNF.
Drinking alone to cope worsens mood and increases risk. Use AUDIT to measure it (NICE CG115) and give brief advice. Alcohol and depression are treated together, not one after the other.

A fit note is legitimate as part of a treatment plan; “may be fit for work” with adjustments is an option. DVLA: depression with significant concentration problems, agitation or suicidal thoughts must be notified by the driver, and he should not drive while affected.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Acknowledges the fit note request but explores before signing; lets him tell the story beyond work.
Breakup, withdrawal from friends and football, drinking alone, work, support from his mum.
Flatness, avoiding eye contact and “everyone’s stressed” are followed rather than accepted.
Idea (work stress); concern (can’t say “I’m depressed”, shame); expectation (a quick note).
Mental state assessment; PHQ-9 to support judgement; AUDIT for alcohol.
Work stress versus depressive episode versus alcohol-related low mood; considers grief after the breakup.
Direct questions on suicidal thoughts, plans, intent, means, past self-harm and protective factors.
Names depression, explains why it is more than stress, and reduces stigma.
NHS Talking Therapies and antidepressant options (NICE NG222) with his preference; fit note as part of care.
Alcohol addressed briefly and without lecturing; driving checked (DVLA); social reconnection encouraged.
Review within a week; crisis routes named; safety plan; risk assessment documented.

social.t: The breakup, withdrawal from football and friends, and drinking alone all remove protective contact. Encourage one step back towards people or activity.
Many men present with physical or practical requests rather than naming low mood. Normalising depression helps them engage.

legal.t: Self-certification covers the first 7 days of sickness; after that a fit note is needed. Consider “may be fit for work” with adjustments such as a phased return or reduced hours.
DVLA: depression with significant memory or concentration problems, agitation, behavioural disturbance or suicidal thoughts must be notified by the licence holder. Advise not driving while affected.

professional.t: Record the direct risk questions and answers, protective factors, the safety plan, crisis numbers given and the review date (NICE NG225).

Occupational health and the Access to Work mental health support service can help with a return. Depression lasting 12 months or more with a substantial effect may count as a disability under the Equality Act 2010.

community.t: NHS Talking Therapies (self-referral); NHS 111 mental health option; Samaritans 116 123; CALM (Campaign Against Living Miserably); Andy’s Man Club peer groups.

redFlags: Suicidal thoughts with a plan, intent, means or preparation
Previous self-harm, escalating alcohol, recent loss, isolation
psychosocial: Breakup of a long-term relationship three months ago
Stopped football, withdrawn from friends; work struggling
ice: Concern: feels a failure and a burden; can’t bring himself to say “depressed”

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “Three months of feeling flat, waking at four, weight loss, giving up things you enjoy and those dark thoughts: that’s depression, not just stress. It’s an illness, and it’s treatable.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Depression is like your battery not charging any more, however long you rest. It changes sleep, appetite and how you see yourself. The right help recharges it.”

management.reflectIce: “You came in saying it’s work stress, and work matters. But I think you knew it was more, and it took courage to tell me about the dark thoughts.”
management.psychosocial: Tie the plan to what he values: his mum, his dog, getting back to football. Keep alcohol advice short and linked to his mood.
sharedPlan: NHS Talking Therapies referral or self-referral; antidepressant as an option with review 1 week after starting (NICE NG222)
Fit note for two weeks as part of treatment; consider adjustments on return
Cut down alcohol with support; one small step back to friends or football
safetyNet: NHS 111 mental health option, Samaritans 116 123, 999 or A&E if he feels unable to keep safe
Review within a week; sooner if thoughts become plans

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: The trap here is the request. Candidates who process the fit note fail the station; candidates who assess but avoid the suicide question fail it too. The patterns below reflect recurring SCA feedback.

items.fail: Signs the fit note for stress and closes.
items.why: “Did not explore the presenting problem.” The depression and the risk are missed entirely.
items.fix: Agree you can help with the note, then ask how things have really been beyond work.

items.fail: Assesses mood thoroughly but never asks directly about suicide.
items.why: “Did not assess risk.” Passive suicidal thoughts are only disclosed when asked.
items.fix: Ask the direct question, then plans, intent, means, past self-harm and protective factors.

items.fail: Starts an antidepressant with review in four weeks.
items.why: NICE NG222: review within 1 week for people at increased risk of suicide.
items.fix: State the 1-week review when discussing medication, and consider overdose toxicity.

items.fail: Labels him as depressed in the first two minutes.
items.why: Premature labelling before he feels heard can make him retreat to “just stress”.
items.fix: Gather his story first, then name depression using his own words back to him.

items.fail: Reacts awkwardly or moves quickly on after the disclosure.
items.why: “Did not respond empathically to the patient’s disclosure.”
items.fix: Pause, thank him, and challenge the burden belief before moving on.

items.fail: Gives generic advice to “seek help if things get worse”.
items.why: Vague safety-netting after suicidal thoughts is a standard failing point.
items.fix: Named crisis routes, when to use each, a review within a week, and teach-back.
